claims.text: A tungsten transition layer can promote a shift from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep in HEA multilayers.
A tungsten transition layer enhances interface coherency in HEA multilayers.
Tungsten provides an intermediate lattice structure that hinders excessive interdiffusion.
The initial HEA multilayers have relatively incoherent interfaces.
Tungsten has a moderate lattice mismatch with the unspecified HEA layers.
Tungsten has a high melting point.
A tungsten interlayer acts as a barrier to atomic diffusion.
A tungsten interlayer reduces interface diffusivity.
Reduced interface diffusivity and increased coherency suppress diffusion-mediated creep processes at high temperatures.
The tungsten interlayer facilitates dislocation-mediated deformation at lower temperatures or higher mechanical loads.
At high temperatures, HEA multilayers containing a tungsten interlayer will have a lower creep rate than otherwise comparable multilayers without tungsten.
At lower temperatures, the dominant creep mechanism in tungsten-containing HEA multilayers will transition to dislocation-mediated behavior.
Diffusion-mediated creep dominates in HEA multilayers without a tungsten transition layer under comparable testing conditions.
The effectiveness of the tungsten interlayer depends on its thickness and deposition quality.
A tungsten layer that is too thin or discontinuous may fail to produce the proposed creep-mechanism transition.
The quantitative creep-rate shift and optimal tungsten-layer thickness are unknown and require experimental validation.
